Electromagnetic waves have two components - electrical fields and magnetic fields. They also have a defining frequency. The way an EM wave interacts with a material is highly based on its frequency - many things that are good shields at a certain frequency are poor shields at others. Metals tend to block out the electrical component of waves, but nothing blocks magnetic fields. However, some materials are more "permeable" to magnetic fields than others, meaning that the magnetic field preferentially travel through that material instead of going into the thing you are trying to shield from magnetic fields. Unalloyed iron is good for this. Mu metal, permalloy, metglass, etc are better, but exponentially more expensive. Think of it like a flood bearing down on your house - you won't stop it, but you can dig a channel around your house that the water can flow through more easily. Interial navigation relies on acceleration, that is then converted into velocity, and finally distance. Any minute errors, noise, or even just estimations when smoothing the data over even the highest of frequencies is going to introduce error that compounds extremely quickly, and that's if your measurement device is absolutely perfect, in reality there is going to be drift (ie, when you move and then stop again, your device is not going to read zero). Your data is absolute rubbish after only a few microseconds, depending on frequency rate. After a few seconds, an inertial sensor tracking movement of a pen across a page, is off by about a foot, depending on input factors.
